newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's cement giant Cemex takes aim at Asia.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's cement giant Cemex takes aim at Asia.

text.p: Mexico-based Cemex SA, one of the world's largest cement markers, is taking aim at booming Asia after previous assaults on the Spanish and Latin American markets.
But in a switch that appeals to cement analysts, the company is not looking to repeat the bumper purchases of the past that made international headlines but also saddled it with enormous debts.

"The capital that we would invest in the first three or four years to go into Asia will be a small amount ... less than two percent of the company's ($3.4 billion) equity," Rodrigo Trevino, CFO at Cemex, told Reuters in a recent interview.

According to the company, its first foray could be announced this quarter. It will not say where, but analysts predict the initial port of call may be Indonesia, where PT Bakrie & Brothers has said it is considering forming a joint-venture cement company with the Mexican firm.

In a further clue that it is putting a strict ceiling on any investment, Cemex says the incursion over the next three years will not cost more than two percent of the group's cash flow, estimated at some $1.25 billion this year.
Cemex says it is the world's third largest cement producer.
Wherever the company goes, analysts said it was not clear whether Cemex would take a minority stake in already existing plants, build a new plant, or administer the business for a third party.
"We can capitalize (on our name) for the benefit of all Cemex shareholders by entering new markets and obtaining administrative or operating contracts that increase returns on capital," Trevino said.
Analysts had worried that Cemex's Asia plans would be a major investment, along the lines of its purchases in Spain, Colombia and Venezuela that have left it highly leveraged.
But Trevino sought to quash that fear. "We want to reassure the markets that indeed we are not going to make a big
Cemex last year went through a major restructuring of some $2.35 billion in debts, but the company's total debt remains high at $5.4 billion.
Its Spanish unit Valenciana de Cementos, raised $850 million in December to refinance debt.

The holding company paid an estimated $700 million last year to gain a controlling interest in Colombia's Cementos Diamante and Industrias e Inversiones Samper, two of the country's largest independent cement makers.

But analysts said it already started showing signs of caution in November last year when it decided not to bid for two Brazilian cement companies because it saw them as too expensive. They welcomed the suggestions that such steadiness would continue in Asia.
"The market is going to take it very well because (it shows) that Cemex is indeed being prudent," said Carmen Slade, analyst at Smith Barney in New York.
"The strategy that Cemex wants to pursue supports my view that the factors that punished the share price in 1996 are no longer valid," she added.
